questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $4$ and $2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-4I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-4I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that the principal components of a standardized observation matrix $X$ are the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$ If 

$$
\lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \cdots\gt \lambda_n
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_1$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue $\lambda_1,$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_2$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue $\lambda_2,$

- $\cdots$

and so on.

For example, suppose that the covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/e40cd1a0df89ba171b921ab971e8eee25e284265df13b7e031ea32fc28d2c27b.svg)

It's easy to show that the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
\lambda_1=10, \qquad
\lambda_2=8.
$$

To find the first principal component of the data, we need the unit eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=10.$ 

Applying our usual algorithm for finding eigenvectors, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}C-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 1 \\ 1 & 9\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/c7050bbb395b939b1b0559b3e7515c4be4f572aed61090f1a4489e126763240f.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/7b0a41deb385aa2471cae701c9f87938085256879a8d834535f8ec0e3f431f27.svg) 

Therefore, the $1$st principal component of the data is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/9490f2e5105592fa3976ae506cbdf64d70c3372d1cc9295eaa6c6580a4ac75aa.svg)

**Note:** The opposite vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/e2b366cfb8cb5b708eb5ba443dfc61c05b498d4eb737b375c8ebc86b96e8eea6.svg) also works in the example above.

tutorials.content:
Recall that the principal components of a standardized observation matrix $X$ are the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C.$ If 

$$
\lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \cdots\gt \lambda_n
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_1$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue $\lambda_1,$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector $\mathbf u_2$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue $\lambda_2,$

- $\cdots$

and so on.

For example, suppose that the covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/e40cd1a0df89ba171b921ab971e8eee25e284265df13b7e031ea32fc28d2c27b.svg)

It's easy to show that the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
\lambda_1=10, \qquad
\lambda_2=8.
$$

To find the first principal component of the data, we need the unit eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=10.$ 

Applying our usual algorithm for finding eigenvectors, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}C-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 1 \\ 1 & 9\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/c7050bbb395b939b1b0559b3e7515c4be4f572aed61090f1a4489e126763240f.svg) 

Finally, dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/7b0a41deb385aa2471cae701c9f87938085256879a8d834535f8ec0e3f431f27.svg) 

Therefore, the $1$st principal component of the data is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/9490f2e5105592fa3976ae506cbdf64d70c3372d1cc9295eaa6c6580a4ac75aa.svg)

**Note:** The opposite vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14199091/assets/e2b366cfb8cb5b708eb5ba443dfc61c05b498d4eb737b375c8ebc86b96e8eea6.svg) also works in the example above.
